strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-designed empirical diagnosis of the 'vision shortcut' phenomenon through three complementary pilot experiments (ID testing, ambiguous LIBERO-Goal scenarios, and OOD SimplerEnv generalization), each isolating a different facet of the failure mode and collectively making a convincing case that goal-driven data collection induces near-vanishing conditional mutual information between instructions and actions.

The Bayesian/PMI formulation is theoretically motivated and cleanly derived (Appendix A), connecting the diagnosed pathology directly to a concrete training objective (LLR maximization) rather than just describing the problem qualitatively.

The Latent Action Query architecture is a neat and practically appealing design: it uses causal masking to cheaply instantiate two conditioning regimes with shared weights, imposes an information bottleneck that decouples DiT complexity from VLM context length, and incurs zero additional inference-time cost, which is empirically substantiated.

Evaluation is broad (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, LIBERO, two independent real-world manipulation setups with blocks and vegetables) and the gains are consistently larger precisely in the ambiguous/OOD conditions the paper's own theory predicts should benefit most (e.g., LIBERO-Goal, SimplerEnv OOD tasks, unseen-color real-world block), which is a meaningful internal consistency check rather than only aggregate improvement.

The ablations are thorough and go beyond simple component removal: they include hyperparameter sweeps (λ, β), query-count sensitivity, and, notably, a well-designed control experiment (auxiliary p(ℓ|v) loss) that helps distinguish 'generic language preservation' from 'action-relevant language grounding,' strengthening the causal story behind the LLR objective.

The qualitative analysis of catastrophic forgetting preservation (Figures 4-6) is a useful side contribution showing the proposed objective has beneficial side effects on retaining general VLM capabilities, an issue of practical relevance to the VLA community.
weaknesses: There are internal numerical inconsistencies that undermine confidence in reported results: the abstract claims an '11.3%' OOD SimplerEnv improvement while the introduction claims '8.8%' improvement for what appears to be the same comparison, and Section 4.5 refers to 'the full LangForce (63.5%)' when Table 5 reports 66.5%, suggesting insufficient proofreading of key quantitative claims.

The practical instantiation of the LLR objective (Eq. 7) is only loosely justified relative to the theoretical PMI decomposition (Eq. 4/12): the paper uses VLM language-modeling loss as a 'proxy' for p(ℓ|a,v) and p(ℓ|v), but the exact correspondence between the causal-masking trick and the target quantities is explained informally in prose rather than rigorously, leaving room for doubt about whether the optimized quantity faithfully approximates PMI or merely encourages some correlated but distinct behavior.

The most directly comparable prior work, BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which also performs a Bayesian decomposition for VLA instruction following, is discussed only qualitatively in related work and is never empirically compared against LangForce in any table, which is a notable gap given how central this comparison would be to establishing the paper's incremental contribution (single-stage vs. two-stage training).

Most reported baseline numbers are taken from original papers rather than reproduced under identical settings; while the authors attempt to control for training data overlap, differences in backbones, compute budgets, and evaluation protocols across papers make some head-to-head comparisons (e.g., against π0.5, Isaac-GR00T-N1.6) less rigorous than a fully controlled ablation would be.

Real-world evaluations use small sample sizes (30 trials per condition) and, for the more interesting OOD conditions, absolute success rates remain low for all methods (e.g., 9/30 and 3/30 for LangForce), which limits the strength of claims about practical OOD generalization despite relative improvements over baselines.

Gains are not uniformly positive across all sub-tasks/settings (e.g., some RoboCasa 'PnP Novel' subsets and some SimplerEnv tasks show baselines or competitors outperforming LangForce), and no statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided for the many success-rate comparisons, making it hard to assess whether some reported differences are meaningful.

strengths: The paper provides a well-organized and fairly convincing set of motivating experiments (Section 2) across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and BridgeDataV2/SimplerEnv that empirically demonstrate the 'vision shortcut' phenomenon, including a clean information-theoretic framing (conditional mutual information / entropy bound) that gives conceptual grounding for the proposed fix.

The core idea of instantiating a Bayesian decomposition via a dual-branch (prior/posterior) architecture sharing weights through causal-masking control of Latent Action Queries is an elegant and computationally cheap mechanism (no extra inference-time cost) that is reasonably well motivated by the PMI/LLR derivation in Appendix A.

Empirical results (Table 1, Table 2) show consistent improvements over the same-framework baseline (QwenGR00T) on both SimplerEnv (55.2% -> 66.5%) and RoboCasa (47.8% -> 50.4%), and the ablation (Table 3) isolates the contribution of Latent Action Queries alone versus the full dual-branch LLR objective, showing both contribute positively.

The qualitative analysis on preservation of general VLM conversational ability (Fig. 4, 5) is an interesting and practically relevant side-benefit that ties into the broader narrative about catastrophic forgetting in VLA fine-tuning.
weaknesses: There is a significant internal inconsistency: BayesianVLA's reported average success rate on SimplerEnv differs between Table 1 (66.5%, per-task 89.6/63.8/33.3/79.2) and Table 3 (63.5%, per-task 81.9/66.6/34.7/70.8) for what appears to be the identical method/backbone/benchmark. This discrepancy is never explained and casts doubt on the reliability and reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The abstract and introduction claim 'extensive experiments... on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa' and Section 4 states evaluation on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2,' but only SimplerEnv and RoboCasa results are actually presented; LIBERO and RoboTwin2 results are absent and explicitly deferred to future work in the Limitations section. This mismatch between claimed and delivered scope suggests the paper was submitted in an unfinished state.

The description of the LLR loss (Eq. 7) and its implementation is underspecified: the text mentions computing a baseline p(ℓ|v) either 'by detaching gradients or using a separate pass,' but the actual mechanism for obtaining this baseline (a full second forward pass without Q? architecture details?) is not clearly specified, harming reproducibility of the central technical contribution.

No statistical significance information (variance across seeds/runs, confidence intervals) is reported for the main results despite running hundreds of trials per task; single-run point estimates are used to claim state-of-the-art performance and precise percentage gains (e.g., '11.3% improvement').

A closely related contemporaneous work with an almost identical framing ('Seeing to act, prompting to specify: A Bayesian factorization of vision language action policy', Xu et al. 2025) is cited only in passing in the catastrophic-forgetting discussion, with no comparison or discussion of how BayesianVLA differs from or improves upon this prior Bayesian-factorization approach to VLA, which undermines the originality claims.

Ablation studies are limited to a single benchmark (SimplerEnv) and a coarse three-way comparison; there is no exploration of key hyperparameters (number of latent queries K, loss weights λ and β) that would clarify sensitivity and robustness of the proposed method.

The claim of 'preserved general capabilities' rests on two anecdotal single-example qualitative comparisons (Fig. 4, 5) rather than any standard multimodal benchmark (e.g., MMBench, MMMU), which is insufficient evidence for the fairly strong claim made in Section 4.3.

Baseline comparisons in Table 1 draw numbers from disparate papers that may use different training data, embodiments, and protocols, which is common practice but is not clearly caveated, making some 'SOTA' claims less rigorous than a fully controlled comparison would allow.
